recipes.name: Delete from a hashed Vec with remove/retain/drain, not swap_remove; pre-size it with with_capacity/reserve
recipes.what: A Vec's order is its index order: remove, retain and drain keep it, swap_remove moves the last element into the hole, and capacity is only a lower bound whose growth the docs leave unspecified.
recipes.how: Pre-size with `Vec::with_capacity(n)` (capacity >= n; the method 'is allowed to allocate for more elements than capacity') or `v.reserve(k)` (capacity >= len + k afterwards). Reuse a per-step buffer with `v.clear()`, which 'has no effect on the allocated capacity'. Remove while keeping order: `v.remove(i)` (shifts the tail, O(n)), `v.retain(|x| keep(x))` (visits each element exactly once in the original order and preserves the order of the retained elements), `v.drain(a..b)` (yields the removed run in order; dropping the Drain unconsumed still removes it). Use `v.swap_remove(i)` (O(1)) only where the order never reaches an output, or sort again before hashing. Never serialise or hash `capacity()`.
recipes.gotchas: `swap_remove(1)` on ['a','b','c','d'] leaves ['a','d','c'] while `remove(1)` leaves ['a','c','d']: same elements, different sequence, different hash. Order-changing removal can also happen inside a dependency: Rapier 0.35.3's graph deletes edges with `edges.swap_remove`, so an iteration order your code never touched still moves. The docs say Vec 'does not guarantee any particular growth strategy when reallocating when full, nor when reserve is called', so `capacity()` after the same pushes is not a portable value. A Drain holds `&mut` on the Vec until it is dropped; leaking it with `mem::forget` may lose elements.
recipes.engine_note: Rapier 0.35.3 removes contact-graph edges with `self.edges.swap_remove(e.index())` (src/data/graph.rs `remove_edge_adjust_indices`), and `NarrowPhase::contact_pairs()` walks that edges vec in index order (`interactions()` -> `raw_edges().iter()`), so pair order changes whenever a contact ends. That is why `rebuild_snapshot` in solver/src/rapier_law.rs collects the pairs into a Vec and sorts them before hashing; it also reuses the snapshot buffer with `out.clear()`, which keeps its capacity.

recipes.name: Let only Vec, VecDeque or BTreeMap/BTreeSet order reach an output; HashMap/HashSet order is random per map
recipes.what: std defines iteration order for sequences (index 0 upward), VecDeque (front to back) and B-trees (key order); HashMap/HashSet iterate in 'arbitrary order' under a randomly seeded hasher that differs per map and per run, and BinaryHeap::iter/into_vec are arbitrary too.
recipes.how: When order can reach bytes, a hash, a log line or a golden, iterate a `Vec`/slice/array (index order), a `VecDeque` (front to back) or a `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (key order; keys must be `Ord`). Keep `HashMap`/`HashSet` to lookups, or collect and sort before emitting: `let mut ks: Vec<_> = m.keys().copied().collect(); ks.sort_unstable();` (map keys are unique, so an unstable sort is safe). Empty a `BinaryHeap` with `pop()` or `into_sorted_vec()` (ascending), never `iter()`/`into_vec()`. Map equality `a == b` ignores order and is safe; `a.iter().eq(b.iter())` compares orders and is not.
recipes.gotchas: Two HashMaps filled by the same inserts in one process iterate differently (measured on 1.98.1), and a second run of the same binary prints yet another order, so a test that compares a run with itself passes. The default hasher is 'currently SipHash 1-3, though this is subject to change at any point in the future': neither std's HashMap order nor its hash values are a persistence contract (fixed-seed hashers, IndexMap and FxHash are covered in float-determinism). `{:?}` of a HashMap follows the same order: the two identical maps printed different Debug text (measured), so never put one in a golden. A BinaryHeap collected from [1, 5, 2, 4, 3] iterates as [5, 4, 2, 1, 3] on 1.98.1: heap array order, not sorted. `BTreeMap<f64, _>` does not compile (E0277, `f64: Ord` is not satisfied).
recipes.engine_note: solver/src (e5fbcb9 and main 4782a8a) holds no HashMap, HashSet or BTreeMap: bodies and colliders live in fixed `static mut` arrays walked in index order, plus `Vec<Option<RigidBodyHandle>>`. Rapier's `contact_pairs()` is Vec-backed but not canonical (see the swap_remove recipe), which is why the snapshot sorts it. Any map added for mesh collision or host bindings should stay off the snapshot path or be a BTreeMap.

recipes.name: Use the map entry API for counters and get-or-insert instead of get_mut followed by insert
recipes.what: `map.entry(k)` searches once and returns an Entry whose `or_insert`, `or_insert_with`, `or_default` and `and_modify` give `&mut V`; the hand-written get_mut / insert / get_mut function that returns the reference is still rejected on 1.98.1 (E0499).
recipes.how: Counter: `*counts.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1;`. Get-or-create that returns a reference: `fn slot(m: &mut HashMap<u32, Vec<u32>>, k: u32) -> &mut Vec<u32> { m.entry(k).or_default() }`. Update-or-insert: `m.entry(k).and_modify(|hp| *hp -= 5).or_insert(100);`. Costly default: `or_insert_with(|| build())` runs the closure only when the key is vacant. BTreeMap has the same API (`btree_map::Entry`).
recipes.gotchas: The get_mut -> insert -> get_mut shape returning `&mut V` is RFC 2094's 'problem case #3'; the RFC text says its analysis handles it, but the borrow checker shipped in 1.98.1 reports E0499 twice for it, so restructure with `entry` rather than fighting the checker. `or_insert(make())` evaluates `make()` on every call, even when the key exists (3 calls for 3 lookups, measured); use `or_insert_with`. `entry(key)` takes the key by value, so a String key is moved even when it is already present. Filling a HashMap through `entry` does not change its arbitrary iteration order.

recipes.name: Give every hashed sort a unique total key; if keys can tie, use stable sort_by, not sort_unstable_by
recipes.what: `sort`, `sort_by` and `sort_by_key` preserve the initial order of equal elements; `sort_unstable*` 'may reorder equal elements', and since the 1.81 switch to ipnsort its docs no longer carry the pdqsort-era promise of 'a fixed seed to always provide deterministic behavior'. With a unique key, both produce identical output.
recipes.how: Make the comparator a total order with no Equal between distinct elements: `v.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| a.key.cmp(&b.key).then(a.id.cmp(&b.id)))`. With such a key the stable and unstable sorts give the same output, so neither an algorithm change nor a toolchain bump can move it. If ties are possible and the key cannot be extended, use stable `sort_by` / `sort_by_key`: equal elements keep their input order, which must itself be canonical. Guard the invariant in tests: `assert!(v.windows(2).all(|w| cmp(&w[0], &w[1]).is_lt()))`.
recipes.rust_version: 1.81+ (driftsort / ipnsort; sorts may panic on a non-total comparator)
recipes.gotchas: Measured on 1.98.1: `sort_unstable_by_key` kept equal keys in input order for 20 elements and reordered them at 21 and 100, so a small unit test hides the difference. Since 1.81 both sorts 'may panic' when the comparator is not a total order, and 'even if the function exits normally, the resulting order of elements in the slice is unspecified'; a cyclic comparator panicked stable `sort_by` on a 50-element input (measured). The 1.82 release notes say the rewritten binary_search 'may select a different value among the equal ones than the old implementation': results that depend on how std treats ties do move between releases.
recipes.engine_note: `rebuild_snapshot` (solver/src/rapier_law.rs, the same at e5fbcb9 and main 4782a8a) sorts `Vec<&ContactPair>` with stable `sort_by` on `(collider1.into_raw_parts(), collider2.into_raw_parts())`. That key cannot tie under Rapier 0.35.3: pair_management.rs adds a contact edge only when the undirected `find_edge(gid1, gid2)` finds none, so each collider pair appears once, and stable or unstable would hash the same bytes. If a later snapshot sorts by a key that can tie (manifold points, a float depth), `sort_unstable_by` would let a move of the 1.98.1 pin reorder tied elements and shift the golden, while `sort_by` would fall back to Rapier's own edge order, which swap_remove rewrites. Extend the key until it is unique instead.

recipes.name: Sort f64 with sort_by(f64::total_cmp), find first matches with partition_point, and dedup floats by bits
recipes.what: f64 is not Ord, so `sort()`, `sort_by_key(|p| p.x)` and `BTreeMap<f64, _>` fail with E0277; `total_cmp` is IEEE 754 totalOrder (-NaN < -inf < ... < -0.0 < +0.0 < ... < +inf < +NaN); on a sorted slice `binary_search` may return any of several equal matches, and `dedup` removes only consecutive PartialEq-equal runs.
recipes.how: `v.sort_by(f64::total_cmp)`; for records `v.sort_by(|a, b| a.depth.total_cmp(&b.depth).then(a.id.cmp(&b.id)))`. Costly keys (a String, a computed norm): `v.sort_by_cached_key(|b| key(b))` calls the key at most once per element (100 calls for 100 elements against 1406 for `sort_by_key`, measured on 1.98.1). First index of a value in a sorted slice: `s.partition_point(|x| *x < target)`; keep `binary_search` for membership or the insertion point (`Err(i)`). Remove every duplicate: sort, then `dedup()`; for floats compare bits: `v.dedup_by(|a, b| a.to_bits() == b.to_bits())`.
recipes.rust_version: total_cmp 1.62+; sort_by_cached_key 1.34+; partition_point 1.52+; binary_search tie choice changed in 1.82
recipes.gotchas: `a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()` panics at the first NaN comparison. `unwrap_or(Ordering::Equal)` is not a total order: on 1.98.1 it made `sort_unstable_by` panic on a 100-element input and left a 1000-element `sort_by` output unsorted without any error (both measured). `total_cmp` puts -0.0 before +0.0 while `==` calls them equal, so `dedup()` collapses [-0.0, 0.0] to the first and never merges NaNs. `[1, 2, 2, 2, 3].binary_search(&2)` returns Ok(3) on 1.98.1, not the first match; the docs say the index 'is chosen deterministically, but is subject to change in future versions of Rust', and 1.82 did change it. The order of sort_by_cached_key's key calls 'is unspecified and may change in future versions'.
recipes.engine_note: `rebuild_snapshot` canonicalises -0.0 to +0.0 in `canon()` before `to_le_bytes` (solver/src/rapier_law.rs), and a NaN makes `write_body` / `canon_quat` refuse, so the step returns false. A future sort by an f64 on the snapshot path (contact points by depth, bodies by distance) should compare the canonicalised values with `total_cmp` plus an id tiebreak; on raw values, -0.0 and +0.0 order differently under `total_cmp`, so the same state could sort differently.

recipes.name: Choose iter, iter_mut or into_iter by ownership, and consume every adapter chain you build
recipes.what: `for x in &v` iterates `&T` (iter), `for x in &mut v` iterates `&mut T` (iter_mut), `for x in v` consumes v and yields `T` (into_iter); adapters such as `map` are lazy and run nothing until consumed; from edition 2021, `array.into_iter()` yields values, while 2015/2018 resolve it to `(&array).into_iter()`.
recipes.how: Read-only pass: `for b in &bodies {}`; in-place update: `for b in &mut bodies { b.v *= k; }`; transfer ownership: `for b in bodies {}` or `bodies.into_iter().map(..).collect()`. Run side effects in a `for` loop or `.for_each(..)`, never a bare `.map(..)`. Arrays in a 2021+ crate: `for x in [a, b, c]` and `[a, b, c].into_iter()` both give values; call `.iter()` when you want references.
recipes.rust_version: array into_iter by value: edition 2021+ (IntoIterator for arrays exists in every edition since 1.53)
recipes.gotchas: `v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));` compiles with `unused_must_use` ('iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed') and `map_unit_fn` warnings and prints nothing. After `for s in v`, `v.len()` is E0382 (v was moved by the loop's implicit `.into_iter()`). In an edition-2018 crate `[1, 2, 3].into_iter().collect::<Vec<i32>>()` is E0277 because the items are `&i32`; code that still compiles there gets the `array_into_iter` lint. Only method-call syntax differs by edition; `for e in [1, 2, 3]` iterates by value in every edition.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml sets `edition = "2021"`, so in the law crate `array.into_iter()` already yields values; the snapshot and step loops walk bodies by index (`for i in 0..loaded.n_bodies`, `while i < n`) rather than through adapters.

recipes.name: Assert equal lengths before zip, handle chunks_exact remainders, and collect into the target you mean
recipes.what: `zip` ends when either input ends, without error; `windows(k)` yields len-k+1 overlapping slices; `chunks_exact(k)` omits the last len % k elements into `remainder()`; `collect` builds any `FromIterator` target: `Result<Vec<_>, E>` stops at the first Err, and a `BTreeMap` sorts by key and keeps one value per key.
recipes.how: `debug_assert_eq!(pos.len(), vel.len()); for (p, v) in pos.iter().zip(&vel) {}`; `for (i, b) in bodies.iter().enumerate()`; `a.iter().chain(&b)` concatenates in order. Fixed strides: `buf.chunks_exact(STRIDE)` and check `.remainder().is_empty()`, or `let (rows, tail) = buf.as_chunks::<17>();` (1.88+, rows are `&[[f64; 17]]`); neighbour pairs: `windows(2)` or `array_windows::<2>()` (1.94+). Parse or refuse: `let xs: Result<Vec<f64>, _> = toks.iter().map(|t| t.parse::<f64>()).collect();`.
recipes.gotchas: Zipping 4 positions with 3 velocities yields 3 pairs and no error. Over 7 items `chunks(3)` gives lengths [3, 3, 1] while `chunks_exact(3)` gives two chunks and hides [7] in `remainder()`. `windows(0)` and `chunks_exact(0)` panic. Collecting into a HashMap or HashSet brings back arbitrary order; into a BTreeMap, duplicate keys keep one value ('all but one of the corresponding values will be dropped'). `collect::<Result<_, _>>()` stops pulling at the first Err, so side effects in the closure stop there too (measured: '1' and 'x' seen, '3' never parsed).
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs lays bodies out as `[f64; MAX_BODIES * BODY_STRIDE]` with BODY_STRIDE = 17 (colliders: COLLIDER_STRIDE = 10), and `body_at` in rapier_law.rs copies a row with an index loop. Over a `&[f64]` view the same rows are `as_chunks::<17>()` with an empty remainder, which puts the stride in the type; how to obtain that view of a `static mut` soundly belongs to the unsafe-ffi lane.

recipes.name: Sum floats in one canonical order: iter().sum() is a left fold from -0.0 and reordering changes the bits
recipes.what: For f16/f32/f64/f128, `Iterator::sum` is `iter.fold(-0.0, |a, b| a + b)` in iteration order (core at tag 1.98.1); float addition is not associative, so reversing or regrouping the same values changes the result, and an empty float sum is -0.0 since 1.82 (rust-lang/rust#129321).
recipes.how: Sum over a canonical sequence (body index order, or a sorted Vec), never over a HashMap/HashSet or a parallel iterator. Choose the identity on purpose: `.sum::<f64>()` starts at -0.0, `.fold(0.0, |a, &b| a + b)` starts at +0.0; they differ only for empty or all -0.0 input. Canonicalise zero before hashing (`if x == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { x }`, then `to_bits()`). If a total must not depend on order, change the representation (integers, fixed point), not the loop.
recipes.gotchas: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3] sums to 0.6000000000000001 forward and 0.6 reversed; [1e16, 1.0, -1e16] sums to 0.0 while [1e16, -1e16, 1.0] sums to 1.0, and the same holds under -O (measured). The fold docs call order 'not important' for 'associative operators like +'; that is true for integers, not for floats. Before 1.82 the float identity was +0.0, so an empty sum hashed through `to_bits()` changes sign across that release. Parallel reductions (rayon) regroup additions (concurrency-async lane).
recipes.engine_note: solver/src contains no `.sum()` today (grep at e5fbcb9 and main 4782a8a). `rebuild_snapshot` sends every f64 through `canon()` (rapier_law.rs), so an empty-sum -0.0 would hash as +0.0 there, while `mix_f64`, which feeds `signature()`, hashes `to_bits()` without canonicalising. Any behaviour number the Phase 2 outcome tests total over bodies should be summed in body-index order.

recipes.name: Return closures as impl Fn with move, and bound callbacks by the weakest Fn trait the call site needs
recipes.what: A closure captures each variable in the first mode its body allows (shared borrow, unique borrow, mutable borrow, move) and implements FnOnce always, FnMut if it moves nothing out, Fn if it also mutates nothing; `move` forces by-value capture (a copy for Copy types) without changing which Fn traits apply.
recipes.how: Return: `fn scaler(k: f64) -> impl Fn(f64) -> f64 { move |x| x * k }`. Parameters: `F: FnOnce()` when you call it once, `FnMut` when it may mutate captured state (std's `retain`, `sort_by` and `map` take FnMut), `Fn` only when it must be callable through `&`. Store different closures as `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(f64) -> f64>>`. A `move` closure over a Copy value copies it and the original stays usable.
recipes.gotchas: Returning `|x| x * k` without `move` is E0373 ('closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `k`'). Calling a closure that moves a capture out a second time is E0382 ('closure cannot be invoked more than once'). The same mistake, a mutating closure passed to an `F: Fn()` parameter, is reported as E0594 when the closure is written inline (the expected bound drives inference), and a closure that only implements FnOnce, bound to a variable first, is reported as E0525. `move` does not make a closure FnOnce. Edition 2021 captures disjoint fields (ownership-borrowing lane).

sources.title: The Rust Reference: Closure types
sources.claim: Capture modes are ImmBorrow, UniqueImmBorrow, MutBorrow and ByValue, chosen as the first mode compatible with the closure body; all closures implement FnOnce, those that move nothing out implement FnMut, those that also mutate nothing implement Fn; move closures may still implement Fn or FnMut.

sources.title: The Rust Reference: Closure expressions
sources.claim: Without move a closure prefers to capture by shared reference; move forces capture by copying or moving, often so the closure's lifetime is 'static.

sources.title: The Rust Programming Language, 13.1 Closures
sources.claim: Closures capture by immutable borrow, mutable borrow or ownership according to what the body does; FnOnce, FnMut and Fn are defined by whether captured values are moved out or mutated.

sources.title: Rust error codes index: E0373
sources.claim: E0373: a captured variable may not live long enough, most commonly when returning a closure that captures a local by reference; the fix is a move closure.

sources.title: Rust error codes index: E0525
sources.claim: E0525: a closure was used where a different Fn trait was expected, e.g. an FnOnce closure passed to a parameter bounded by Fn.

recipes.name: Treat str lengths as bytes, slice only on char boundaries, and keep Unicode case mapping out of hashed keys
recipes.what: String and &str are always valid UTF-8: `len()` counts bytes, `s[i]` does not compile (E0277), `&s[a..b]` panics off a char boundary while `s.get(a..b)` returns None, and Unicode-aware methods follow `char::UNICODE_VERSION`, which the docs say changes over time without that being a breaking change.
recipes.how: Take `&str` parameters, return `String` when you allocate. Count chars with `s.chars().count()`, walk bytes with `s.bytes()`, find cut points with `s.char_indices()` or `s.is_char_boundary(i)`, slice with `s.get(a..b)`. Decode untrusted bytes with `String::from_utf8(bytes)` (Err on invalid input); `from_utf8_lossy` silently substitutes U+FFFD. For names or ids that reach a hash, compare with `eq_ignore_ascii_case` / `to_ascii_lowercase` or on raw bytes, not with `to_lowercase`. `format!("{:>8.3}", x)`: width 8, and for floats precision is the number of digits after the decimal point.
recipes.gotchas: `"héllo".len()` is 6 and `.chars().count()` is 5; `&s[0..2]` panics ('end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)'). `to_uppercase` can change length ('Straße' becomes 'STRASSE') and its tables follow `UNICODE_VERSION`, (17, 0, 0) on 1.98.1, so a toolchain bump can change case mapping. `{}` printed 1e21 as 1000000000000000000000 (measured). Formatted float text is not a hashing format; hash bits (float-determinism lane).
